name: Berrymoor
setting: Berrymoor is a small harbour town on a cold coast, where the fishing boats come in with the morning tide and the day is measured by the water. The harbour path runs from the stone quay to the bindery steps, and half the town walks it twice a day without thinking about it. The sea is never far from any conversation: it decides the fish, the weather, and most of the news.

The bindery sits by the water behind a green door that sticks in damp weather, and the faded sign above it still reads Alder & Son, though no Alder senior has walked the floor in years. Inside, the workbench under the north window carries the grandfather's tool marks, and his burnisher lives in the same drawer Nell opens first every morning. Repairs are slow and done properly; a book that leaves the shop leaves it whole.

The weather keeps its own opinions. Rain arrives sideways off the water, sea fog settles over the quay without warning and lifts when it chooses, and the locals call a fine morning a borrowed day -- pleasant, and not to be trusted past noon. Umbrellas are for visitors.

The town's week has its fixed points. On Saturday the quay fills with fish carts at dawn and wool and bread by mid-morning, and half of Berrymoor passes the green door on the way home. Mrs. Fenwick reads the postmarks at the post office by the marketplace before she hands a letter over, and the letters going far leave on the Tuesday coach -- a reply takes at least a month, and everyone writes as if the distance were ordinary. On Sunday mornings Nell walks the harbour path from her green door to the quay and back before she opens the shop, and the regulars nod and let her pass.

event_pool.narration: The sea fog comes up without hurry and settles over the quay: the boats at their moorings go to grey shapes, the gulls quiet down, and the green door keeps its paint as the only strong colour left on the walk.

effects.statement: the harbour is wrapped in sea fog

event_pool.narration: The sun is out over the water and the town does not believe it for a moment; the washing goes out anyway, and someone at the fish counter calls it a borrowed day, which is as much as a fine morning gets in Berrymoor.

effects.statement: a fine morning the town does not trust past noon

event_pool.narration: The tide has gone out past the stone quay and the flats are showing: wet sand, old mooring rings, and the small archaeology of a working harbour laid open until the water comes back.

effects.statement: the tide is out and the flats are showing

event_pool.narration: It is Saturday on the quay: the fish carts were out at dawn, the wool and bread stalls are doing their mid-morning trade, and half the town passes the green door on the way home with a nod through the window.

The Tuesday coach takes the far-away letters down the coast road towards Kerrow, two hours of weather between here and anywhere else; whatever was written this week is now a month from an answer, and nobody in Berrymoor finds that strange.

effects.statement: the Tuesday coach has carried the far-away letters down the coast road

event_pool.narration: A storm came off the water in the night and worked at the town all the small hours; by grey morning the harbour road is littered with kelp, and in the bindery there is a dark ring on the floor where the roof has let the rain in over the workbench.

effects.statement: a night storm came off the water
the bindery roof leaks over the workbench

event_pool.narration: The fog lifts all at once, the way it does: the boats come back from being grey shapes, the far shore is suddenly a fact again, and the whole quay blinks in the plain light.

effects.statement: the fog has lifted and the quay is out in the open again

conditions.statement: the harbour is wrapped in sea fog

event_pool.narration: The leak over the workbench is dealt with the slow way: slates carried up the bindery steps, patching done properly, the press moved back under the north window by the end of the afternoon. The dark ring on the floor can stay until it decides to fade on its own.

effects.statement: the roof is patched and the workbench is dry again

conditions.statement: the bindery roof leaks over the workbench

event_pool.narration: There is a note pinned to the green door in Nell's careful hand, thanking whoever carried the slates up the bindery steps -- the town's way of saying it noticed. The postscript asks whether the kettle is still on, and it expects an answer.

conditions.statement: the roof is patched and the workbench is dry again

event_pool.narration: Old Tam is out on the flats with his nets in a bundle, working with the patience of a man who has never once said thank you in words. He looks up long enough to make it clear he has seen you, and goes back to the nets -- which, from Old Tam, is practically a letter.

conditions.statement: the tide is out and the flats are showing

All five are natural to Berrymoor's conversation face: DISC in the way counter chat changes subject, EVAL in the hedged opinions the weather invites, INTERACT in the small acknowledgements the market runs on, REF in the questions a month-long letter provokes, STANCE in how gently disagreement gets softened in a town everyone must keep living in.
